newsitem.title: USA: Old people less likely to get costly care - study.
newsitem.headline: Old people less likely to get costly care - study.

text.p: Old people are much less likely to get aggressive, high-cost and often futile medical care at the end of life than commonly believed, a panel of experts on aging and death said Monday.
They said the popular misconceptions about end-of-life care could steer the national debate about health-care costs in an unwise and unfair direction.

Taking care of the elderly can be costly, but the costs are not predominantly wasteful, high-tech hospital care, according to the study sponsored by the Alliance for Aging Research and the Open Society Institute's Project on Death in America.

The report comes as lawmakers near a resolution to the short-term financial problems of Medicare, and begin to turn their attention to coping with millions of aging baby-boomers who will start hitting retirement age early in the next century.
It also comes as the Supreme Court considers two cases about the constitutionality of physician-assisted suicide. A ruling is expected in July.

Alliance director Daniel Perry said that underneath the national debate about health spending there is an image lurking of "very ill, very old people at the end of life" consuming more than their "fair share" of Medicare dollars.

"The fastest growing segment of the U.S. population -- the oldest of the old -- may be the least of our worries in controlling health care," he said. "The fact is, the cost of dying drops sharply as people age so that Medicare costs for Americans 85 and older are the lowest for any age group during the last year of life."

The panel prepared a report called the "Seven Deadly Myths" about the last year of life, and said the No. 1 misconception is that older people commonly receive heroic, high-tech treatments at the end of life.

In fact, fewer than half of all people over age 65 die in the hospital, and the older people are, the less likely they are to receive aggressive care when dying, said Dr. Gene Cohen, chairman of the study panel and head of the Center of Aging, Health and Humanities at George Washington University.
The experts estimated that even if care had been cut off to the 3.5 percent of Medicare users in 1993 who had the highest costs, it would have saved $5 billion out of a $900 billion program.

And when elderly people do receive aggressive care, it is not necessarily futile. Many get to live longer, and it is extremely difficult for doctors to accurately predict who is really terminally ill or on the brink of death.
The experts said the medical field must develop better prognostic tools to help patients and their families make decisions about care.

Dr. Kathleen Foley, an expert on cancer pain control at Memorial Sloan-Kettering in New York and the director of the Project on Death in America, said doctors must also learn to better recognize and treat pain and depression in the elderly and the terminally ill.
